explanations.answer: They both fall into a pit
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus asks, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). The question lands on both of them, not just one. That's what makes it such a sharp picture.

Nice try, friend, but turning back home isn't in what Jesus says. He asks, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). The question ends with a pit. I'd love a happy ending here too, but that's not the picture He paints.

explanations.answer: They both wait by the road
explanations.explanation: Waiting sounds peaceful, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. His question is, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). The parable has the two of them falling into a pit together.

Close, baker, but Jesus says the opposite. He says, "A disciple is not above his teacher…" (Luke 6:40). A disciple is a learner, someone following a teacher. So the answer is False, and the learner doesn't outrank the one teaching him.

Right, baker. Jesus says, "A disciple is not above his teacher…" (Luke 6:40). The learner isn't over the one teaching him. A disciple is a learner following a teacher, and that's the order Jesus gives.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "…everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher." (Luke 6:40). Fully trained is the key. A disciple who finishes his training becomes like the one who taught him.

A good guess, friend, but a father isn't who Jesus names here. He says everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher (Luke 6:40). The whole line is about a disciple and the one training him. Nobody's family tree comes into it.

Not this time, friend. Jesus says the fully trained one will be like his teacher (Luke 6:40). Brothers do show up in the next verse, but that's a different picture. Here it's all about a disciple and his teacher.

That's it, baker. A speck is tiny, and a beam is a big heavy piece of timber. Jesus sets them side by side in Luke 6:41, and the size gap is the whole picture. It's like a single sprinkle next to a full oven rack, and somebody's only worried about the sprinkle.

A thorn does sting, friend, but it's not what Jesus names. He says a beam is in your own eye (Luke 6:41). A thorn is small, and a beam is huge. Thorns come back in Luke 6:44, though, with the thornbushes.

A hair in the eye would ruin anybody's day, friend. But Jesus says the word is beam (Luke 6:41). That's a big piece of timber sitting in your own eye. A little hair would be a much smaller problem than that.

That's what Jesus calls him, baker. He says, "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). He's talking to someone who offers to help his brother with a speck while he can't see the beam in his own eye. It's a word for somebody whose offer doesn't match his own situation.

Fool is a strong word, friend, but it isn't the one Jesus uses here. In this verse He says, "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). That's the name for the one offering to remove a speck while a beam sits in his own eye.

Not that one, friend. Jesus says, "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). He says it to someone who offers to take a speck out of his brother's eye while a beam sits in his own. The word scoffer doesn't show up in this verse.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye." (Luke 6:42). Notice the order. Your own eye comes first, and then you can see clearly to help your brother.

This one is True, friend. Jesus says, "First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye." (Luke 6:42). He doesn't say to skip helping your brother. He puts your own eye first, so you can see clearly for the job.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says, "No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit." (Luke 6:43). So a bad tree growing something good doesn't happen in His picture. The answer is False, and the tree and its fruit go together.
Right, baker. Jesus says, "No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit." (Luke 6:43). It goes both directions. Good trees and their fruit match, and so do bad trees and theirs.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit." (Luke 6:44). What a tree grows tells you what kind of tree it is. Then He adds that figs aren't gathered from thornbushes, nor grapes from brambles.

Roots are important, friend, but they're not the word Jesus uses. He says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit." (Luke 6:44). Fruit is what you can see and gather. He follows with figs and grapes, which are fruit too.
Leaves are a fair guess, friend, but Jesus points to something else. He says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit." (Luke 6:44). Then He mentions figs and grapes, which are fruit, not leaves.

explanations.answer: The good treasure of his heart
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart…" (Luke 6:45). The source is his heart. What comes out of him starts there.

explanations.answer: The good work of his hands
explanations.explanation: Hands are busy, friend, but that's not what Jesus names. He says the good man brings good things out of "…the good treasure of his heart…" (Luke 6:45). The source is the heart, and the good things come out from there.

explanations.answer: The good store in his house
explanations.explanation: I like the picture of a full storeroom, friend. But Jesus says the good man brings good things out of "…the good treasure of his heart…" (Luke 6:45). The treasure isn't in his house. It's in his heart.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." (Luke 6:45). Picture a mixing bowl filled to the top. Whatever's inside is what spills over, and in this verse that spill is what the mouth says.

The mind is a good guess, friend, but Jesus uses a different word. He says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." (Luke 6:45). Earlier in that same verse He speaks of the treasure of the heart. What comes out of the mouth is the overflow of the heart.

Spirit sounds right to me too, friend, but it's not Jesus' word. He says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." (Luke 6:45). The same verse speaks of the good treasure and the evil treasure of the heart. The mouth speaks out of the overflow of the heart.

That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?" (Luke 6:46). Saying the words and doing what He says are two different things. I think that question lands softly and still hits hard.

Praying in private isn't what Jesus mentions here, friend. He asks, "Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?" (Luke 6:46). The question is about not doing what He says. Praying isn't in it.

That's a good thing to care about, friend, but it's not in this question. Jesus asks, "Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?" (Luke 6:46). The words are about calling Him Lord and not doing what He says. He doesn't name any one thing.

That's right, baker. Jesus says the one who comes to Him, hears His words and acts on them is "…like a man building a house…" (Luke 6:48). It's a builder's picture. And a builder is somebody who's actually doing something.
A vineyard is a nice picture, friend, but Jesus doesn't use it here. In this parable He says the man is building a house (Luke 6:48). He dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock.
Sheep are a Bible favorite, friend, but not here. Jesus says the one who hears and acts is like a man building a house (Luke 6:48). It's about digging and building, with no flock in the picture.
That's the one, baker. Jesus says the man "…dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock." (Luke 6:48). He didn't skip the digging and he didn't stop early. The rock is where the house sits.

Sand shows up in a lot of people's memories of this story, friend, but Luke's version doesn't say it. Luke 6:48 says the man "…laid his foundation on the rock." The other builder in Luke 6:49 has ground without a foundation.
A hill sounds like a fine building spot, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention one. He says the man "…dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock." (Luke 6:48). The rock is the word to hold onto.
Close, baker, but the torrent doesn't win this round. Jesus says it "…crashed against that house but could not shake it…" (Luke 6:48). So the answer is False. The house on the rock stood.
Right, baker. Jesus says the torrent "…crashed against that house but could not shake it…" (Luke 6:48). It hit hard, and the house didn't move. The flood really came and the house still held.

You got it, baker. Jesus says the torrent "…could not shake it, because it was well built." (Luke 6:48). The text gives that reason. The house stood because of how it was built, right down to the foundation on the rock.

Small isn't what Jesus says, friend. He says, "When the flood came, the torrent crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built." (Luke 6:48). The reason the text gives is how the house was built.

That's an interesting thought, friend, but Jesus doesn't say where the man was. He says the torrent "…could not shake it, because it was well built." (Luke 6:48). The reason belongs to the house, with nothing said about the man.

That's right, baker. Jesus says this man "…built his house on ground without a foundation." (Luke 6:49). The first builder dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock. This one skipped that part.
A roof is handy in a flood, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention one. He says the man built on "…ground without a foundation." (Luke 6:49). It's what's under the house that matters.
A door is nice, friend, but that's not the missing piece here. Jesus says the man built his house "…on ground without a foundation." (Luke 6:49). The missing piece is the foundation.
That's it, baker. Jesus says, "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell…" (Luke 6:49). No leaning and no waiting around. It went down right away.

That would be a lucky house, friend, but Jesus says something different. "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell…" (Luke 6:49). It doesn't lean and it doesn't stand, it falls. Jesus also adds that great was its destruction.
Slow would've given somebody time, friend, but Jesus says "immediately." His words are, "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell…" (Luke 6:49). It was quick.
